snippet.textDisplay: Left my job of 20 yrs  6 yrs ago to care for my father (who just turned 90), my uncle who will be 84, my mother in law who is 79. Also cared for 79 yr old father in who passed away a year ago, an aunt who passed away 3 yrs ago and a cousin who passed 2 yrs ago. I will be 58 in December. This has been more difficult than working 9 to 5. This is 24/7. Trying to schedule everyone's doctor's appointments, surgeries, medications, and errands is daunting. We all need to remember how important it is to care for ourselves in order to give the best care to our loved ones. Prayers to everyone in this phase of life.

snippet.textDisplay: I am 61 years old. I am a c.n.a. who works only in dementia. My mom is 85 years old. She was doing ok until she had heart attack. Was put under for stints. Then she broke ankle, was put under for pins in ankle. She hasnt been the same since. Being put under has changed her. She now has early stages of dementia. Tough to watch and deal with, and work with dementia residents all day. It is hard on all families when the children now have to be the parents of the parents and the roles switch. Yes, it is consuming!

snippet.textDisplay: My parents and I have been living together for the past year.  We have each made adjustments.  I think this is a sacred time, a chance for me, Mom, and Dad to reacquaint ourselves.  I am 65, and they are 85 and 86.  I would encourage anyone who can or who is willing to give this a chance.  I can still remember my parents taking care of me, and now we look out for each other.  My maternal grandmother had her mom and mother-in-law, along with several children, in one home. I hope we find every opportunity to enjoy our parents in this stage of their lives.  I am fortunate to have this time here.  BTW I moved into their home on my way to Africa, and I made the right decision to just stay put.

snippet.textDisplay: Thank you so much for making this statement out loud! It has consumed my life. I had to resign from my career in aviation, and that was nine years ago.. I’m sitting here at his bedside. He is currently in Hospice and had a stroke this afternoon. I am so deprived of sleep of rest of just life. It’s so easy for people to say you have to take care of yourself but at what point in time do you actually get to do that? Would someone please explain this to me? What am I doing wrong? Nothing. This is exactly what it is and it is completely overwhelming. You can’t leave. you can’t quit. You can’t walk away. You can take breaks…little ones. I have been praying for my dad’s body to release and for him to pass on. He’s been in state for at least a year that is not very dignifying and he doesn’t want to be here. He doesn’t want to live. We need to have laws in place so that our elders can pass when they choose, if they choose. Godspeed for big Jim, please. 🙏🌀✨🌀❤️

I’m 59 and my brother 60. We have been dealing with our Mom for the last 19 years and dementia is the strangest disease. She has lived with both of us and is unhappy even-though we are giving everything up for her.
We feel like we can’t win.

snippet.textDisplay: Went through this about 5 years ago initially trying to help my suicidal stepdaughter . Then my mom got ill so I took turns with my other siblings flying out and caring for her in another state while she went through chemo, then repeating it the next year as she went through hospice. Then repeated the whole scenario again with my mother-in-law in yet another state. Multiple trips for my father-in-law who fortunately has the live - in help of my sister-in-law. But my sister-in-law has lupus, so we know she will eventually need our help. My father is almost 80, so I know that is coming. Meanwhile I've been going through menopause, and then a health crisis of my own that I still haven't recovered from or figured out.  I don't know what I was thinking when I was younger, I thought life would actually get easier after 50, thought we would be in a better place financially, the kids would be grown up and independent, and we could breathe. I'm realizing now that life is never going to get easier, it just seems to get harder and harder.

Then my mom got ill so I took turns with my other siblings flying out and caring for her in another state while she went through chemo, then repeating it the next year as she went through hospice. Then repeated the whole scenario again with my mother-in-law in yet another state. Multiple trips for my father-in-law who fortunately has the live - in help of my sister-in-law. But my sister-in-law has lupus, so we know she will eventually need our help. My father is almost 80, so I know that is coming. Meanwhile I've been going through menopause, and then a health crisis of my own that I still haven't recovered from or figured out.  I don't know what I was thinking when I was younger, I thought life would actually get easier after 50, thought we would be in a better place financially, the kids would be grown up and independent, and we could breathe. I'm realizing now that life is never going to get easier, it just seems to get harder and harder.

snippet.textDisplay:
I’m so sorry to hear of dementia. I’m 63 now, and the youngest of 3. Back in the day, my mom had me when she was 38!
People made comments to her at that time, but we would laugh that she set the standard.
Now my dad passed at 91, because of his heart, he had pleurisy so badly they put in a port. Both of my parents passed w full cognition. My dad, was in his hospice bed, yelling at us who were in another room to not forget something having to do w $! He had a great sense of hearing! His body was slowly going, his knees, then lack of muscle strength- which got him more upset but I told him, you can look at your great grandchildren and know who they are… I would want that. My dad passed a week before my parents 70th anniversary. I was 54. Only a few months later did my mom’s hairdresser see that she was jaundice.
Arguments ensued between myself & my sister. My mom did have a blockage in her pancreas but while in the hospital, no oncologist came to see her, so I thought she’s ok. But in the beginning of 2017, they finally told her & us she had pancreatic cancer. She didn’t have any extra surgery only palliative radiation - and she was good for 15 months, she passed a month after Christmas where she was laughing & joking & celebrating her 94th birthday. They were Italian and ate Italian! There was NEVER any chips or junk food in our house! And my dad owned a grocery store. I was 55 when she passed. Now my sister, who was 77 died earlier this year, of ovarian cancer and don’t still know if it started in her colon bc the year before she had it out.
Her kids 54 & 53 & still doing paperwork. So ours happened really early but thank God they were on their own until they were 88/89.
My best to everyone, I know the meds schedule & drs visits & blood tests.
There are many NPs who are now doing wellness visits & house calls.
If you have a home healthcare worker; please watch them, some w hidden cameras bc I’ve had 2 friends who found 1 of the workers to be stealing from their parents. That’s sad. Take care… one who’s been there. 💕

snippet.textDisplay:
I have an 80 year old mom with dementia. She is weak, has poor balance, sometimes agitated or apathetic, no longer drives, and gets lost. I take her to hair and nail appointments, lunch out of the house, shopping which is very confusing for her so I do a lot of her shopping. Dr appointments, I take notes and make sure she takes her meds, the right amount at the right time. We have to make sure she eats, drinks water and takes short walks. She has someone that helps with house work, laundry, cleaning, yard work.

All this while having a job I’m spending less time at and trying to navigate my first year of menopause and the changes that accompany that.

I have to think there are many of us in this space and time of life. It is a difficult path to navigate. I didn’t anticipate this at all. Balancing the care of my aging parents with caring for myself and my young adult kids.

Also, we all quit drinking, got rid of the alcohol, to help my mom with overconsumption and really for me, to focus on taking care of my body, brain, mental and emotional health. It can be really easy to lean on alcohol to help deal with the stress instead of self soothing in healthy ways.

Even though my mom and I have had some friction in our relationship over the years, I and my family choose to love her every day and take care of her the best we can. Some days are better than others.
💕

snippet.textDisplay:
I’m 59. I’ve been caring for my frail, demented mom since 2017. Running 2 households. Trying to help my own children become productive adults (which happens much later now than previous generations).
She is 93. When she was 60, she was winning medals in Senior Olympic events. She was taking hormones prescribed by her dr. (80’s-90’s). At 70, still athletic and independent (though she did not strength train EVER) with stage 2 pelvic prolapse, she was yanked from hormones after the WHI announcement. In the next 12-15 years she had both hips replaced, and began suffering spinal compression fractures, idiopathic myocarditis, vertigo, and dementia. Her prolapse progressed to stage 4. By age 85, she was dependent on a rollator and a caregiver.
Yes- I hear you! My own prolapse journey is what led me to you. And Dr. Casperson. And the meno-posse!
Because of strength of women like you, I am learning about the medical injustices inflicted on generations of women.
Remember- we are the generation that will change this world. Keep educating. Keep eating. Keep lifting. Keep advocating. We love you.
I keep saying this is the hardest stage of my life because in order for me to move on, I have to lose my mother. 😢
